title: A Tiny Snail's Teeth on a Rock Are Stronger Than Spider Silk
hook: Limpet teeth scored higher than spider silk, once the strongest biological material

open.title: A seashore snail took the strongest biological material record
open.line: A cone-shaped shell clings tight to a rock on the shore. This small snail has a record hiding in its mouth.

summary: Limpets scrape algae off rocks with iron mineral fiber teeth. A 2015 study measured them stronger than spider silk.

text: A cone-shaped shell clings tight to a rock on the shore.
It's a limpet, a shore-dwelling sea snail.
A limpet has rows of teeth on a tongue-like organ.
It scrapes algae off rock with them.

panels.text: Scraping rock and the teeth don't chip?

text: It has over 100 rows of teeth but eats with only the outer 10.
Worn teeth break down within 12 to 48 hours.
UK researchers gathered Southampton limpets and measured their teeth.
A single tooth is less than 1 mm long.
They cut a tiny piece of tooth and pulled it with an atomic force microscope.
Its strength came out between 3.0 and 6.5 gigapascals.
Actually, that's higher than spider silk.
Spider silk had been the strongest biological material.
The secret is goethite inside the teeth.
Very thin iron mineral fibers tightly fill a protein frame.
The team said they could inspire materials for cars, boats, planes and dentistry.

sources: Royal Society: Limpet teeth have super strength (2015)
Barber et al. (2015) Extreme strength observed in limpet teeth, Journal of the Royal Society Interface 12: 20141326
